citation.sourceDocument: Arizona DOR 2026 Form 140ES booklet — 2.5% flat rate; standard deduction conformed to the federal amounts (A.R.S. §43-1041)
citation.sourceNote: Arizona finished its move to a single flat rate in 2023 and has held it at 2.5% since; the 2026 Form 140ES worksheet says it outright — 'Multiply line 18 by 2.5% (.025) to calculate your Arizona estimated tax liability.' Arizona sets its OWN standard deduction in A.R.S. §43-1041(A) and indexes it by §63's method — subsection (H) adjusts the amounts "in the same manner in which the federal BASIC standard deduction is adjusted" — so the figures track the federal ones without being them, and this shard carries the 2026 $16,100 / $32,200 / $24,150. The distinction is not academic: "basic" excludes §63(f)'s aged and blind additional, which Arizona does not import. It gives its own instead — $2,100 per person aged 65 and $1,500 per blind person, taken as exemptions on Form 140 lines 38-39 rather than added to the deduction — and that is NOT modeled here, so a 65-year-old Arizonan's deduction reads low by $2,100. There is no Arizona personal exemption. Worked example, single $60,000: taxable = 60,000 − 16,100 = $43,900; tax = 2.5%·43,900 = $1,097.50. Omitted at launch fidelity: the STANDARD DEDUCTION INCREASE, an Arizona-only addition of a percentage of charitable contributions (34% for 2025) on top of the standard deduction for filers who do not itemize — so a charitable filer's real deduction is larger and this figure errs high; the dependent tax credit; and Arizona's other credits. Arizona levies no local income tax. Verified against the Arizona DOR 2026 Form 140ES booklet on 2026-08-29.
